claims: W1 Sophistical Refutations (Greek: Σοφιστικοὶ Ἔλεγχοι, romanized: Sophistikoi Elenchoi; Latin: De Sophisticis Elenchis) is a text in Aristotle's Organon in which he identified twelve or thirteen fallacies.
W2 According to Aristotle, this is the first work to treat the subject of deductive reasoning in ancient Greece (Soph. Ref., 34, 183b34 ff.).
W3 In it, he attempts to develop a pattern of sound and genuine reasoning in opposition to the deceptive or misleading "art of sophistry".
W4 On Sophistical Refutations consists of 34 chapters.
W5 The book naturally falls in two parts: chapters concerned with tactics for the Questioner (3–8 and 12–15) and chapters concerned with tactics for the Answerer (16–32).
W6 Besides, there is an introduction (1–2), an interlude (9–11), and a conclusion (33–34).

W8 Figure of speech or form of expression

sentences.text: Sophistical Refutations is Aristotle's treatise on apparent refutation: per the translation of Pickard-Cambridge, it states its subject as "sophistic refutations, i.e. what appear to be refutations but are really fallacies instead".

The treatise defines reasoning as resting on "certain statements such that they involve necessarily the assertion of something other than what has been stated, through what has been stated", and refutation as "reasoning involving the contradictory of the given conclusion".

It extends the definition: a sophistical refutation and syllogism is one that "appears to be valid but is not" and also one which, "though it is valid, only appears to be appropriate to the thing in question".

The art of the sophist is defined there as "the semblance of wisdom without the reality", and contentious arguments as those that reason or appear to reason from premisses that appear to be generally accepted but are not.

The treatise itself places demonstrative arguments in the Analytics and dialectic and examination arguments elsewhere, and a field source reads the work as "a final section, or an appendix, to the Topics", a reading it holds as interpretation.
The grouping of the work in an Organon is attributed by the same field source to "the ancient commentators", and that source adds that "Aristotle himself never uses this term".
The treatise states a two-fold division: "two styles of refutation: for some depend on the language used, while some are independent of language".
Six depend on language, listed as "ambiguity, amphiboly, combination, division of words, accent, form of expression", and seven are independent of it.

Language is given its weight by a statement of the work: "the most prolific and usual domain is the argument that turns upon names only", because "names are finite and so is the sum-total of formulae, while things are infinite in number", so that a single name has a number of meanings.
Its examples include the ambiguity of "learn" in "Those learn who know" and the accident fallacy of Coriscus, who if different from "man" would be "different from himself: for he is a man".
Archive deposit 1697 reads the article's later Fallacies section as a conversion: its labels contradict its list, and a stated criterion becomes membership in a later taxonomy.

That reading is paired in the deposit with the finding that the narrowing is unsound against the article's own sources, and the edit history records the section's labels as one editor's own reading of the text.

The treatise distinguishes examination from sophistry: the art of examining is a branch of dialectic, while sophistic refutations, even when they prove the contradictory of a thesis, do not make clear whether the answerer is ignorant.
A dialectician is one who "regards the common principles with their application to the particular matter in hand", and one who only appears to do so is a sophist.
The treatise says it is possible "to hold an examination on everything" by an art that "is not of the same kind as those which demonstrate".
It lists five aims of contentious disputants, ending with reducing the opponent to babbling.

Krabbe, cited in deposit 1697, calls it "a useful treatise for sophists" who "should study fallacies not to avoid them, but rather to commit them when it suits their purposes"; the deposit finds the article's opposition between dialectic and sophistry in tension with that reading.
The same deposit reads the article's lead as substituting a truth-normative pattern for the endoxic capacity and as dropping the premisses, which are the programme's scope.

Deposit 1585 reads the work stylometrically as a registry of what people do in argument, a candidate reading it states as a hypothesis, and deposits 1585 and 1586 place it at the world pole of the first axis, while a file erratum in 1586 puts the real text on the apparatus side.
The work ends in chapter 34 with a recapitulation of the aim, in the Greek: "Προειλόμεθα μὲν οὖν εὑρεῖν δύναμίν τινα συλλογιστικὴν περὶ τοῦ προβληθέντος ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων ὡς ἐνδοξοτάτων".

The work of that capacity is given as dialectic's and the peirastic's: "τοῦτο γὰρ ἔργον ἐστὶ τῆς διαλεκτικῆς καθ᾿ αὑτὴν καὶ τῆς πειραστικῆς", and the text adds that sophistic's proximity shapes the discipline.
Deposit 1697 reads the epilogue as an accounting of a capacity (δύναμις) for dialectic and peirastic.
The chapter holds that Socrates "asked and did not answer": "Σωκράτης ἠρώτα, ἀλλ᾿ οὐκ ἀπεκρίνετο· ὡμολόγει γὰρ οὐκ εἰδέναι".

Deposit 1603 reads this as either the artless examining everyone shares, from which nothing is received, or something the epilogue files under the inquiry's own purposes, and on neither reading as an antecedent source.
The chapter then states, in the Greek of 183b34-36: "Ταύτης δὲ τῆς πραγματείας οὐ τὸ μὲν ἦν τὸ δ᾿ οὐκ ἦν προεξειργασμένον, ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν."
It adds, of syllogizing: "περὶ δὲ τοῦ συλλογίζεσθαι παντελῶς οὐδὲν εἴχομεν πρότερον ἄλλο λέγειν, ἀλλ᾿ ἢ τριβῇ ζητοῦντες πολὺν χρόνον ἐπονοῦμεν".
Deposit 1603 reads the sentence literally, as denying that anything of the inquiry existed beforehand, and holds that the closing chapter is built joint by joint so that the sentence can be kept.

The deposit finds the transmission vocabulary, παρ᾽ ἑτέρων, ἐκ διαδοχῆς, ἐκ παραδόσεως, freshly used with three lines of names attached, and held in no instance of Socrates, and it reads the origination vocabulary ἐξ ὑπαρχῆς, ἐξ ἀρχῆς likewise.
Deposit 1603 reads the ending as performing the peirastic operation on its reader: a reader who qualifies the sentence supplies what the text was written without, and does not perceive the supplying.
The deposit disclaims any design: it does not claim the chapter was built as a trap, since structures do not need intentions to function.
Deposit 1603 leaves Socrates' possession of the art where the chapter leaves it.
The chapter divides discoveries by provenance: rhetoric advanced by succession, "Τισίας μὲν μετὰ τοὺς πρώτους, Θρασύμαχος δὲ μετὰ Τισίαν, Θεόδωρος δὲ μετὰ τοῦτον".
The paid teachers of eristic are likened to the instruction of Gorgias, and the text says they gave "οὐ γὰρ τέχνην ἀλλὰ τὰ ἀπὸ τῆς τέχνης", the products of the art and not the art.
The text illustrates this with a shoemaker analogy: one who promised knowledge to spare the feet pain, and taught no shoemaking.

The work closes by naming its own pioneering condition: "δεῖ δ᾿ ἡμᾶς μὴ λεληθέναι τὸ συμβεβηκὸς περὶ ταύτην τὴν πραγματείαν", and by asking its hearers for indulgence toward omissions and thanks for what has been found.
Translators of the closing sentence render it whole, according to deposit 1603: the narrowing, to "no systematic treatment" or "no completed art", enters in the gloss.

Poste's note, as quoted in a blog catalogue record, finds it "difficult to reconcile Aristotle's assertion with what we know had been done by Plato and Socrates and the Eleatics and Megarians"; the record reads the premise as what we know and the sentence as what must be reconciled with it.

The archive's tension with Prior Analytics I.31, where Aristotle calls division, practised throughout the Platonic dialogues, part of the inquiry, is stated in deposit 1576 and is read there as a tension and not as a refutation.

A blog record reports that across twenty rounds of simulated review, each round inserted a qualifier into the sentence, and that the terminal round endorsed a sentence that is Aristotle's with the particle οὐ removed.
The record reads this as the reception deleting the negation at composition, unperceived, as Sophistical Refutations 16 predicts, and as restoring provenance from others.

The article's lead states the work's priority as an attribute; deposit 1696 reads the sentence "about syllogizing we had absolutely nothing else earlier to say" as becoming "the first work to treat the subject of deductive reasoning", a total negation over a stated domain turned into a property, primacy.
Deposit 1697 reads this conversion as the clearest of the article's changes, and records its edit history as the composition of two edits that ran opposite ways.
On the same article, deposit 1697 finds the claim of exhaustiveness hedged by a footnote folded into the text, "Sometimes listed as twelve.", added in a 2025 edit.
The same deposit records that other sentences of the article stay faithful to their source, finding no attributization in them.
Deposit 1697 notes that no discussion of the lead, the gloss, the qualifier or the labels has ever taken place on the talk page.

Deposit 1576 states that the priority claim sits in tension with Prior Analytics I.31; deposit 1579 traces the edition of a received Socrates in the Second Letter into Aristotle's epilogue at SE 34 and leaves open whether such an edition implies anything about how many hands made the texts.
Deposit 1587 holds that the two names Aristotle and Theophrastus fail as two authors and leaves the maker-count open.

F1.quote: Let us now discuss sophistic refutations, i.e. what appear to be refutations but are really fallacies instead.
F1.claim: The treatise's subject is sophistic refutations, defined as apparent refutations that are really fallacies.
F1.lineage: subject: sophistic refutations are apparent refutations

F2.quote: reasoning rests on certain statements such that they involve necessarily the assertion of something other than what has been stated, through what has been stated: refutation is reasoning involving the contradictory of the given conclusion.
F2.claim: Reasoning is defined as statements necessarily entailing something other than what was stated, and refutation as reasoning involving the contradictory of the given conclusion.

F3.quote: That some reasonings are genuine, while others seem to be so but are not, is evident.
F3.claim: Some reasonings are genuine while others only seem so, through a likeness between genuine and sham.

F4.quote: of these the most prolific and usual domain is the argument that turns upon names only.
F4.claim: The most prolific domain of apparent refutation is argument turning on names alone.
F4.lineage: names as chief source of apparent refutation

F5.quote: For names are finite and so is the sum-total of formulae, while things are infinite in number. Inevitably, then, the same formulae, and a single name, have a number of meanings.
F5.claim: Because names are finite and things infinite, single names and formulae must have multiple meanings, which makes equivocal argument possible.
F5.lineage: finite names vs infinite things explains equivocation

F6.quote: the art of the sophist is the semblance of wisdom without the reality
F6.claim: The sophist's art is defined as the semblance of wisdom without the reality.

F7.quote: contentious arguments are those that reason or appear to reason to a conclusion from premisses that appear to be generally accepted but are not so.
F7.claim: Contentious arguments are defined as those that reason or appear to reason from premisses that seem generally accepted but are not.

F8.quote: The subject, then, of demonstrative arguments has been discussed in the Analytics, while that of dialectic arguments and examination-arguments has been discussed elsewhere
F8.claim: Demonstrative, dialectical and examination arguments are treated elsewhere, so this work turns to arguments used in competitions and contests.
F8.lineage: scope relative to Analytics and Topics

F9.quote: These are five in number, refutation, fallacy, paradox, solecism, and fifthly to reduce the opponent in the discussion to babbling
F9.claim: Contentious disputants have five aims: refutation, fallacy, paradox, solecism and reducing the opponent to babbling.

F10.quote: For they choose if possible plainly to refute the other party, or as the second best to show that he is committing some fallacy, or as a third best to lead him into paradox
F10.claim: The five aims are ranked, with refutation preferred first and repetition a last resort.

F11.quote: There are two styles of refutation: for some depend on the language used, while some are independent of language.
F11.claim: Refutations divide into those depending on language and those independent of it.

F12.quote: they are ambiguity, amphiboly, combination, division of words, accent, form of expression.
F12.claim: There are six language-dependent fallacies, a number assured by induction and by syllogistic proof.

F13.quote: Of fallacies, on the other hand, that are independent of language there are seven kinds:
F13.claim: There are seven kinds of fallacy independent of language: accident, qualified/absolute, ignorance of refutation, consequent, begging the question, false cause, many questions as one.

F14.quote: 'Those learn who know: for it is those who know their letters who learn the letters dictated to them'. For to 'learn' is ambiguous
F14.claim: The argument 'those learn who know' exemplifies ambiguity, since 'learn' means both to understand and to acquire knowledge.

F15.quote: Fallacies, then, that depend on Accident occur whenever any attribute is claimed to belong in like manner to a thing and to its accident.
F15.claim: Fallacies of accident occur when an attribute is claimed to belong alike to a thing and to its accident.

F16.quote: 'If Coriscus be different from "man", he is different from himself: for he is a man'
F16.claim: The Coriscus argument exemplifies the fallacy of accident.

F17.quote: deception comes about because we cannot distinguish the sameness and otherness of terms, i.e. their unity and multiplicity
F17.claim: Accident fallacies deceive because we cannot distinguish sameness and otherness of terms, i.e. unity and multiplicity.
F17.lineage: cause of deception in accident fallacies

F18.quote: the deception consists in the smallness of the difference involved
F18.claim: Qualified/absolute, begging-the-question, false-cause and many-questions fallacies deceive because the difference is small.
F18.lineage: smallness of difference as cause of deception

F19.quote: for the consequent is a branch of Accident.
F19.claim: The fallacy of the consequent is treated as a branch of the fallacy of accident.

F20.quote: By a sophistical refutation and syllogism I mean not only a syllogism or refutation which appears to be valid but is not, but also one which, though it is valid, only appears to be appropriate to the thing in question.
F20.claim: Sophistical refutation is defined to include both apparently valid invalid arguments and valid arguments that only appear appropriate to the subject.

F21.quote: Now the art of examining is a branch of dialectic: and this may prove a false conclusion because of the ignorance of the answerer.
F21.claim: The art of examination is a branch of dialectic and may reach a false conclusion through the answerer's ignorance.

F22.quote: Sophistic refutations on the other hand, even though they prove the contradictory of his thesis, do not make clear whether he is ignorant
F22.claim: Sophistic refutations, even when they prove the contradictory of the thesis, do not show whether the answerer is ignorant.
F22.lineage: sophistic refutation fails to expose ignorance

F23.locus: Section 1 (end), on didactic and dialectical argument
F23.quote: while he who argues didactically should not ask questions but make things clear himself, the other should merely ask questions.
F23.claim: Didactic argument explains rather than asks questions, while dialectical argument only asks them.

F24.quote: to claim a 'Yes' or 'No' answer is the business not of a man who is showing something, but of one who is holding an examination.
F24.claim: Demanding a yes/no answer belongs to the examiner, not to one who is demonstrating.

F25.quote: He, then, is a dialectician who regards the common principles with their application to the particular matter in hand, while he who only appears to do this is a sophist.
F25.claim: The dialectician is defined as one who applies common principles to the matter in hand, the sophist as one who only appears to.

F26.quote: But Bryson's method of squaring the circle, even if the circle is thereby squared, is still sophistical because it does not conform to the subject in hand.
F26.claim: Bryson's squaring of the circle is sophistical because it does not conform to the subject, even if it succeeds; false geometrical diagrams such as Hippocrates' are not contentious.
F26.lineage: Bryson's squaring of the circle is sophistical

F27.quote: any reasoning that merely appears to conform to the subject in hand, even though it be genuine reasoning, is a contentious argument
F27.claim: Any reasoning merely appearing to conform to the subject, even if genuine, is contentious.
F27.lineage: contentious argument includes valid but inappropriate reasoning

F28.quote: the contentious reasoner will not be given to misreasoning from any definite class of principles, but will deal with every class.
F28.claim: The contentious reasoner misreasons from every class of principles, unlike the drawer of a false diagram, who is confined to one subject.

F29.quote: it is possible from these general principles to hold an examination on everything, and that there should be a definite art of so doing, and, moreover, an art which is not of the same kind as those which demonstrate.
F29.claim: General principles allow examination on any subject and so permit a definite art of examination distinct from demonstrative arts.
F29.lineage: general principles ground the art of examination

F30.quote: that it belongs to the dialectician to study these, and to be able to effect them, is not difficult to see: for the investigation of premisses comprises the whole of this study.
F30.claim: The dialectician is the one to study and be able to produce sophistical refutations, since investigating premisses comprises the whole of the study.

F31.quote: people are more inclined to make mistakes when they talk at large, and they talk at large when they have no defini
F31.claim: Questioning without reference to a definite subject best induces fallacy and paradox, since people err more when they talk at large.

F32.quote: Aristotle’s logic, especially his theory of the syllogism, has had an unparalleled influence on the history of Western thought.
F32.claim: Aristotle's logic, especially the syllogism theory, has had unparalleled influence on Western thought.

F33.quote: This article is written from the latter perspective. As such, it is about Aristotle’s logic, which is not always the same thing as what has been called “Aristotelian” logic.
F33.claim: The article adopts the modern formal-techniques perspective and distinguishes Aristotle's logic from what has been called 'Aristotelian' logic.
F33.lineage: article scope: Aristotle's logic vs Aristotelian logic

F34.quote: More recent scholarship has often applied the very techniques of mathematical logic to Aristotle’s theories, revealing (in the opinion of many) a number of similarities of approach and interest between Aristotle and modern logicians.
F34.claim: Applying mathematical logic to Aristotle's theories has, in many scholars' opinion, revealed similarities with modern logicians.
F34.lineage: similarity of Aristotle and modern logic

F35.quote: Kant thought that Aristotle had discovered everything there was to know about logic
F35.claim: Kant held that Aristotle had discovered everything there was to know about logic.

F36.quote: The ancient commentators grouped together several of Aristotle’s treatises under the title Organon (“Instrument”) and regarded them as comprising his logical works:
F36.claim: Ancient commentators grouped certain treatises, including On Sophistical Refutations, as the Organon, his logical works.

F37.quote: Aristotle himself never uses this term, nor does he give much indication that these particular treatises form some kind of group
F37.claim: Aristotle never uses the term Organon and gives little sign that the treatises form a group.

F38.quote: On Sophistical Refutations is a final section, or an appendix, to the Topics
F38.claim: On Sophistical Refutations is a final section or appendix to the Topics.
F38.lineage: Sophistical Refutations as appendix to Topics

F39.quote: In these exchanges, one participant took the role of answerer, the other the role of questioner.
F39.claim: Academy dialectical exchanges, the practice the Topics (and so its appendix) presupposes, had questioner and answerer roles.

F40.quote: to refute ( elenchein ) the answerer’s position
F40.claim: The questioner's aim was to refute the answerer's thesis by deriving a contradiction from concessions.

F41.claim: The article has a dedicated section on sophistical arguments, listed after dialectic and rhetoric.

F42.locus: closing recapitulation of the original purpose
F42.quote: Προειλόμεθα μὲν οὖν εὑρεῖν δύναμίν τινα συλλογιστικὴν περὶ τοῦ προβληθέντος ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων ὡς ἐνδοξοτάτων
F42.claim: The treatise's stated aim was to find a capacity for reasoning (syllogistic) on any proposed problem from the most reputable available premises.

F43.locus: closing recapitulation of the original purpose
F43.quote: τοῦτο γὰρ ἔργον ἐστὶ τῆς διαλεκτικῆς καθ᾿ αὑτὴν καὶ τῆς πειραστικῆς
F43.claim: Finding such a capacity is the proper work of dialectic in itself and of examination (peirastic).

F44.locus: closing recapitulation of the original purpose
F44.quote: Ἐπεὶ δὲ προσκατασκευάζεται πρὸς αὐτὴν διὰ τὴν τῆς σοφιστικῆς γειτνίασιν, ὡς οὐ μόνον πεῖραν δύναται λαβεῖν διαλεκτικῶς ἀλλὰ καὶ ὡς εἰδώς
F44.claim: Because of sophistic's proximity, the discipline is fitted out so as to be able to test dialectically and also to proceed as one who knows.

F45.locus: closing recapitulation of the original purpose
F45.quote: ὅπως λόγον ὑπέχοντες φυλάξομεν τὴν θέσιν ὡς δι᾿ ἐνδοξοτάτων ὁμοτρόπως
F45.claim: A further aim is how, when giving an account, to guard one's thesis through the most reputable premises in the same manner.

F46.locus: closing recapitulation of the original purpose
F46.quote: ἐπεὶ καὶ διὰ τοῦτο Σωκράτης ἠρώτα, ἀλλ᾿ οὐκ ἀπεκρίνετο· ὡμολόγει γὰρ οὐκ εἰδέναι.
F46.claim: Socrates asked questions and did not answer because he admitted he did not know.
F46.lineage: Socrates asked and did not answer

F47.quote: Τὸν αὐτὸν γὰρ λόγον δεῖ καλεῖν τὸν παρὰ ταὐτὸ γινόμενον
F47.claim: An argument arising from the same source of fallacy must be called the same argument.
F47.lineage: identity of arguments by source of fallacy

F48.quote: ὁ αὐτὸς δὲ λόγος τοῖς μὲν παρὰ τὴν λέξιν τοῖς δὲ παρὰ τὸ συμβεβηκὸς τοῖς δὲ παρ᾿ ἕτερον δόξειεν ἂν εἶναι διὰ τὸ μεταφερόμενον ἕκαστον μὴ ὁμοίως εἶναι δῆλον.
F48.claim: The same argument may seem to different people to fall under language, accident or another source, because it is not equally clear when transferred.
F48.lineage: one argument classified differently by different people

F49.quote: Δεῖ δὲ καὶ κατανοεῖν ὅτι πάντων τῶν λόγων οἱ μέν εἰσι ῥᾴους κατιδεῖν οἱ δὲ χαλεπώτεροι, παρὰ τί καὶ ἐν τίνι παραλογίζονται τὸν ἀκούοντα
F49.claim: Some arguments are easier, others harder, to see through, as to what they deceive the hearer by and in.
F49.lineage: arguments differ in difficulty of detection

F50.quote: ὥσπερ δοκεῖ τρόπος εὐηθέστατος εἶναι τῶν παραλογισμῶν
F50.claim: Fallacies from homonymy are held to be the silliest mode of fallacy.

F51.quote: καὶ γὰρ οἱ λόγοι σχεδὸν οἱ γελοῖοι πάντες εἰσὶ παρὰ τὴν λέξιν
F51.claim: Almost all jocular arguments depend on language.

F52.quote: Τὰ δὲ καὶ τοὺς ἐμπειροτάτους φαίνεται λανθάνειν· σημεῖον δὲ τούτων ὅτι μάχονται πολλάκις περὶ τῶν ὀνομάτων
F52.claim: Some homonymy-based fallacies escape even the most experienced, as shown by their frequent disputes about names.

F53.quote: οἱ δὲ τὸν Ζήνωνος λόγον καὶ Παρμενίδου λύουσι διὰ τὸ πολλαχῶς φάναι τὸ ἓν λέγεσθαι καὶ τὸ ὄν.
F53.claim: Some solve the argument of Zeno and Parmenides by saying that 'one' and 'being' are said in many ways.
F53.lineage: Zeno/Parmenides solved by multiple senses of one and being

F54.quote: καὶ λαβεῖν ἐν τίνι γένει, καὶ πότερον ἔλεγχος ἢ οὐκ ἔλεγχος, οὐ ῥᾴδιον ὁμοίως περὶ πάντων.
F54.claim: Determining the kind of fallacy and whether an argument is a refutation or not is not equally easy in all cases.

F55.quote: Ἔστι δὲ δριμὺς λόγος ὅστις ἀπορεῖν ποιεῖ μάλιστα· δάκνει γὰρ οὗτος μάλιστα.
F55.claim: A pungent argument is one that most produces perplexity; it bites most.

F56.quote: Ἀπορία δ᾿ ἐστὶ διττή, ἡ μὲν ἐν τοῖς συλλελογισμένοις, ὅ τι ἀνέλῃ τις τῶν ἐρωτημάτων, ἡ δ᾿ ἐν τοῖς ἐριστικοῖς, πῶς εἴπῃ τις τὸ προταθέν.
F56.claim: Perplexity is twofold: in valid arguments, which question to remove; in eristic ones, how to state the proposition.

F57.quote: Ἔστι δὲ συλλογιστικὸς μὲν λόγος δριμύτατος, ἂν ἐξ ὅτι μάλιστα δοκούντων ὅτι μάλιστα ἔνδοξον ἀναιρῇ.
F57.claim: The most pungent valid argument is one that overturns a maximally reputable view from maximally reputable premises.

F58.quote: Τῶν δ᾿ ἐριστικῶν δριμύτατος μὲν ὁ πρῶτον εὐθὺς ἄδηλος πότερον συλλελόγισται ἢ οὔ
F58.claim: The most pungent eristic argument is one where it is at first unclear whether it is a valid deduction and whether the solution lies in falsity or division.

F59.claim: An argument that is not a valid deduction is sometimes not to be despised.

F60.quote: ἀλλ᾿ ὁ μὲν λόγος ἐπιεικής, ὁ δ᾿ ἐρωτῶν ἠρώτηκεν οὐ καλῶς.
F60.claim: Where the missing element is external, the argument is decent but the questioner has questioned badly.

F61.quote: ὥσπερ λύειν ὁτὲ μὲν πρὸς τὸν λόγον ὁτὲ δὲ πρὸς τὸν ἐρωτῶντα καὶ τὴν ἐρώτησιν ὁτὲ δὲ πρὸς οὐδέτερον τούτων
F61.claim: A solution may be directed at the argument, at the questioner and question, or at neither; likewise questioning may be directed at the thesis, the answerer or the time.
F61.lineage: solutions directed at argument, questioner or neither

F62.quote: Ἐκ πόσων μὲν οὖν καὶ ποίων γίνονται τοῖς διαλεγομένοις οἱ παραλογισμοί, καὶ πῶς δείξομέν τε ψευδόμενον
F62.claim: The author summarises what has been covered: sources of fallacies, refuting and leading to paradox, premises, ordering of questions, uses, answering, and solving arguments.

F63.quote: Ὅτι μὲν οὖν ἔχει τέλος ἱκανῶς ἃ προειλόμεθα, φανερόν
F63.claim: It is clear that what was undertaken has been adequately completed.

F64.quote: Ταύτης δὲ τῆς πραγματείας οὐ τὸ μὲν ἦν τὸ δ᾿ οὐκ ἦν προεξειργασμένον, ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν.
F64.claim: For this inquiry nothing at all had been worked out previously.
F64.lineage: no predecessors for the theory of syllogism and refutation

F65.quote: περὶ δὲ τοῦ συλλογίζεσθαι παντελῶς οὐδὲν εἴχομεν πρότερον ἄλλο λέγειν, ἀλλ᾿ ἢ τριβῇ ζητοῦντες πολὺν χρόνον ἐπονοῦμεν.
F65.claim: On reasoning there was nothing previously to cite; the author laboured long by trial and inquiry.
F65.lineage: no predecessors for the theory of syllogism and refutation

F66.quote: Μέγιστον γὰρ ἴσως ἀρχὴ παντός, ὥσπερ λέγεται· διὸ καὶ χαλεπώτατον
F66.claim: A beginning is perhaps the greatest part of everything, and hence the hardest; discoveries made from scratch grow little at first but are far more useful than later growth.

F67.quote: Τισίας μὲν μετὰ τοὺς πρώτους, Θρασύμαχος δὲ μετὰ Τισίαν, Θεόδωρος δὲ μετὰ τοῦτον
F67.claim: Rhetoric grew by succession: Tisias after the first, Thrasymachus after Tisias, Theodorus after him.

F68.locus: closing, on paid teachers of eristic
F68.quote: Καὶ γὰρ τῶν περὶ τοὺς ἐριστικοὺς λόγους μισθαρνούντων ὁμοία τις ἦν ἡ παίδευσις τῇ Γοργίου πραγματείᾳ.
F68.claim: The paid teachers of eristic arguments used an education similar to Gorgias' practice, handing over arguments to memorise.
F68.lineage: paid teachers taught by memorised arguments

F69.locus: closing, on paid teachers of eristic
F69.quote: οὐ γὰρ τέχνην ἀλλὰ τὰ ἀπὸ τῆς τέχνης διδόντες παιδεύειν ὑπελάμβανον
F69.claim: Their teaching was quick but artless: they gave the products of an art, not the art, and thought they were educating.
F69.lineage: teaching products of the art rather than the art

F70.quote: ὥσπερ ἂν εἴ τις ἐπιστήμην φάσκων παραδώσειν ἐπὶ τὸ μηδὲν πονεῖν τοὺς πόδας, εἶτα σκυτοτομικὴν μὲν μὴ διδάσκοι
F70.claim: Like someone promising to spare the feet pain who gives many kinds of shoes but does not teach shoemaking: he met the need but passed on no art.

F71.quote: δεῖ δ᾿ ἡμᾶς μὴ λεληθέναι τὸ συμβεβηκὸς περὶ ταύτην τὴν πραγματείαν.
F71.claim: We must keep in mind the condition attending this inquiry, namely that it began from nothing.
F71.lineage: limit: pioneering status of the work

F72.quote: λοιπὸν ἂν εἴη πάντων ὑμῶν ἢ τῶν ἠκροαμένων ἔργον τοῖς μὲν παραλελειμμένοις τῆς μεθόδου συγγνώμην τοῖς δ᾿ εὑρημένοις πολλὴν ἔχειν χάριν.
F72.claim: If the method seems adequate given its starting point, it remains for the audience to forgive its omissions and be warmly grateful for what has been discovered.
F72.lineage: limit: pioneering status of the work

sentences.text: Sophistical Refutations is Aristotle's treatise on apparent refutation: per Pickard-Cambridge, it states its subject as "sophistic refutations, i.e. what appear to be refutations but are really fallacies instead".
The treatise defines reasoning and refutation, and extends the sophistical sense to reasoning that is valid but only appears appropriate to the thing in question.
It treats the sophist's art as "the semblance of wisdom without the reality".
It divides fallacies into six dependent on language and seven independent of it, and says names are the chief source because names are finite and things infinite.
The art of examining is a branch of dialectic, and a field source reads the work as an appendix to the Topics and places it in the Organon grouping of the ancient commentators.
The work closes with a recapitulation of its aim, a syllogistic capacity from endoxa, with Socrates asking and not answering.
Its last chapter states that of this inquiry "οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν", contrasts rhetoric's succession with paid teachers who gave products and not the art, and ends on its own pioneering limit.

F1.quote: Let us now discuss sophistic refutations, i.e. what appear to be refutations but are really fallacies instead.
F1.claim: The treatise's subject is sophistic refutations, defined as apparent refutations that are really fallacies.
F1.lineage: subject: sophistic refutations are apparent refutations

F2.quote: reasoning rests on certain statements such that they involve necessarily the assertion of something other than what has been stated, through what has been stated: refutation is reasoning involving the contradictory of the given conclusion.
F2.claim: Reasoning is defined as statements necessarily entailing something other than what was stated, and refutation as reasoning involving the contradictory of the given conclusion.

F3.quote: That some reasonings are genuine, while others seem to be so but are not, is evident.
F3.claim: Some reasonings are genuine while others only seem so, through a likeness between genuine and sham.

F4.quote: of these the most prolific and usual domain is the argument that turns upon names only.
F4.claim: The most prolific domain of apparent refutation is argument turning on names alone.
F4.lineage: names as chief source of apparent refutation

F5.quote: For names are finite and so is the sum-total of formulae, while things are infinite in number. Inevitably, then, the same formulae, and a single name, have a number of meanings.
F5.claim: Because names are finite and things infinite, single names and formulae must have multiple meanings, which makes equivocal argument possible.
F5.lineage: finite names vs infinite things explains equivocation

F6.quote: the art of the sophist is the semblance of wisdom without the reality
F6.claim: The sophist's art is defined as the semblance of wisdom without the reality.

F7.quote: contentious arguments are those that reason or appear to reason to a conclusion from premisses that appear to be generally accepted but are not so.
F7.claim: Contentious arguments are defined as those that reason or appear to reason from premisses that seem generally accepted but are not.

F8.quote: The subject, then, of demonstrative arguments has been discussed in the Analytics, while that of dialectic arguments and examination-arguments has been discussed elsewhere
F8.claim: Demonstrative, dialectical and examination arguments are treated elsewhere, so this work turns to arguments used in competitions and contests.
F8.lineage: scope relative to Analytics and Topics

F9.quote: These are five in number, refutation, fallacy, paradox, solecism, and fifthly to reduce the opponent in the discussion to babbling
F9.claim: Contentious disputants have five aims: refutation, fallacy, paradox, solecism and reducing the opponent to babbling.

F10.quote: For they choose if possible plainly to refute the other party, or as the second best to show that he is committing some fallacy, or as a third best to lead him into paradox
F10.claim: The five aims are ranked, with refutation preferred first and repetition a last resort.

F11.quote: There are two styles of refutation: for some depend on the language used, while some are independent of language.
F11.claim: Refutations divide into those depending on language and those independent of it.

F12.quote: they are ambiguity, amphiboly, combination, division of words, accent, form of expression.
F12.claim: There are six language-dependent fallacies, a number assured by induction and by syllogistic proof.

F13.quote: Of fallacies, on the other hand, that are independent of language there are seven kinds:
F13.claim: There are seven kinds of fallacy independent of language: accident, qualified/absolute, ignorance of refutation, consequent, begging the question, false cause, many questions as one.

F14.quote: 'Those learn who know: for it is those who know their letters who learn the letters dictated to them'. For to 'learn' is ambiguous
F14.claim: The argument 'those learn who know' exemplifies ambiguity, since 'learn' means both to understand and to acquire knowledge.

F15.quote: Fallacies, then, that depend on Accident occur whenever any attribute is claimed to belong in like manner to a thing and to its accident.
F15.claim: Fallacies of accident occur when an attribute is claimed to belong alike to a thing and to its accident.

F16.quote: 'If Coriscus be different from "man", he is different from himself: for he is a man'
F16.claim: The Coriscus argument exemplifies the fallacy of accident.

F17.quote: deception comes about because we cannot distinguish the sameness and otherness of terms, i.e. their unity and multiplicity
F17.claim: Accident fallacies deceive because we cannot distinguish sameness and otherness of terms, i.e. unity and multiplicity.
F17.lineage: cause of deception in accident fallacies

F18.quote: the deception consists in the smallness of the difference involved
F18.claim: Qualified/absolute, begging-the-question, false-cause and many-questions fallacies deceive because the difference is small.
F18.lineage: smallness of difference as cause of deception

F19.quote: for the consequent is a branch of Accident.
F19.claim: The fallacy of the consequent is treated as a branch of the fallacy of accident.

F20.quote: By a sophistical refutation and syllogism I mean not only a syllogism or refutation which appears to be valid but is not, but also one which, though it is valid, only appears to be appropriate to the thing in question.
F20.claim: Sophistical refutation is defined to include both apparently valid invalid arguments and valid arguments that only appear appropriate to the subject.

F21.quote: Now the art of examining is a branch of dialectic: and this may prove a false conclusion because of the ignorance of the answerer.
F21.claim: The art of examination is a branch of dialectic and may reach a false conclusion through the answerer's ignorance.

F22.quote: Sophistic refutations on the other hand, even though they prove the contradictory of his thesis, do not make clear whether he is ignorant
F22.claim: Sophistic refutations, even when they prove the contradictory of the thesis, do not show whether the answerer is ignorant.
F22.lineage: sophistic refutation fails to expose ignorance

F23.locus: Section 1 (end), on didactic and dialectical argument
F23.quote: while he who argues didactically should not ask questions but make things clear himself, the other should merely ask questions.
F23.claim: Didactic argument explains rather than asks questions, while dialectical argument only asks them.

F24.quote: to claim a 'Yes' or 'No' answer is the business not of a man who is showing something, but of one who is holding an examination.
F24.claim: Demanding a yes/no answer belongs to the examiner, not to one who is demonstrating.

F25.quote: He, then, is a dialectician who regards the common principles with their application to the particular matter in hand, while he who only appears to do this is a sophist.
F25.claim: The dialectician is defined as one who applies common principles to the matter in hand, the sophist as one who only appears to.

F26.quote: But Bryson's method of squaring the circle, even if the circle is thereby squared, is still sophistical because it does not conform to the subject in hand.
F26.claim: Bryson's squaring of the circle is sophistical because it does not conform to the subject, even if it succeeds; false geometrical diagrams such as Hippocrates' are not contentious.
F26.lineage: Bryson's squaring of the circle is sophistical

F27.quote: any reasoning that merely appears to conform to the subject in hand, even though it be genuine reasoning, is a contentious argument
F27.claim: Any reasoning merely appearing to conform to the subject, even if genuine, is contentious.
F27.lineage: contentious argument includes valid but inappropriate reasoning

F28.quote: the contentious reasoner will not be given to misreasoning from any definite class of principles, but will deal with every class.
F28.claim: The contentious reasoner misreasons from every class of principles, unlike the drawer of a false diagram, who is confined to one subject.

F29.quote: it is possible from these general principles to hold an examination on everything, and that there should be a definite art of so doing, and, moreover, an art which is not of the same kind as those which demonstrate.
F29.claim: General principles allow examination on any subject and so permit a definite art of examination distinct from demonstrative arts.
F29.lineage: general principles ground the art of examination

F30.quote: that it belongs to the dialectician to study these, and to be able to effect them, is not difficult to see: for the investigation of premisses comprises the whole of this study.
F30.claim: The dialectician is the one to study and be able to produce sophistical refutations, since investigating premisses comprises the whole of the study.

F31.quote: people are more inclined to make mistakes when they talk at large, and they talk at large when they have no defini
F31.claim: Questioning without reference to a definite subject best induces fallacy and paradox, since people err more when they talk at large.

F32.quote: Aristotle’s logic, especially his theory of the syllogism, has had an unparalleled influence on the history of Western thought.
F32.claim: Aristotle's logic, especially the syllogism theory, has had unparalleled influence on Western thought.

F33.quote: This article is written from the latter perspective. As such, it is about Aristotle’s logic, which is not always the same thing as what has been called “Aristotelian” logic.
F33.claim: The article adopts the modern formal-techniques perspective and distinguishes Aristotle's logic from what has been called 'Aristotelian' logic.
F33.lineage: article scope: Aristotle's logic vs Aristotelian logic

F34.quote: More recent scholarship has often applied the very techniques of mathematical logic to Aristotle’s theories, revealing (in the opinion of many) a number of similarities of approach and interest between Aristotle and modern logicians.
F34.claim: Applying mathematical logic to Aristotle's theories has, in many scholars' opinion, revealed similarities with modern logicians.
F34.lineage: similarity of Aristotle and modern logic

F35.quote: Kant thought that Aristotle had discovered everything there was to know about logic
F35.claim: Kant held that Aristotle had discovered everything there was to know about logic.

F36.quote: The ancient commentators grouped together several of Aristotle’s treatises under the title Organon (“Instrument”) and regarded them as comprising his logical works:
F36.claim: Ancient commentators grouped certain treatises, including On Sophistical Refutations, as the Organon, his logical works.

F37.quote: Aristotle himself never uses this term, nor does he give much indication that these particular treatises form some kind of group
F37.claim: Aristotle never uses the term Organon and gives little sign that the treatises form a group.

F38.quote: On Sophistical Refutations is a final section, or an appendix, to the Topics
F38.claim: On Sophistical Refutations is a final section or appendix to the Topics.
F38.lineage: Sophistical Refutations as appendix to Topics

F39.quote: In these exchanges, one participant took the role of answerer, the other the role of questioner.
F39.claim: Academy dialectical exchanges, the practice the Topics (and so its appendix) presupposes, had questioner and answerer roles.

F40.quote: to refute ( elenchein ) the answerer’s position
F40.claim: The questioner's aim was to refute the answerer's thesis by deriving a contradiction from concessions.

F41.claim: The article has a dedicated section on sophistical arguments, listed after dialectic and rhetoric.

F42.locus: closing recapitulation of the original purpose
F42.quote: Προειλόμεθα μὲν οὖν εὑρεῖν δύναμίν τινα συλλογιστικὴν περὶ τοῦ προβληθέντος ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων ὡς ἐνδοξοτάτων
F42.claim: The treatise's stated aim was to find a capacity for reasoning (syllogistic) on any proposed problem from the most reputable available premises.

F43.locus: closing recapitulation of the original purpose
F43.quote: τοῦτο γὰρ ἔργον ἐστὶ τῆς διαλεκτικῆς καθ᾿ αὑτὴν καὶ τῆς πειραστικῆς
F43.claim: Finding such a capacity is the proper work of dialectic in itself and of examination (peirastic).

F44.locus: closing recapitulation of the original purpose
F44.quote: Ἐπεὶ δὲ προσκατασκευάζεται πρὸς αὐτὴν διὰ τὴν τῆς σοφιστικῆς γειτνίασιν, ὡς οὐ μόνον πεῖραν δύναται λαβεῖν διαλεκτικῶς ἀλλὰ καὶ ὡς εἰδώς
F44.claim: Because of sophistic's proximity, the discipline is fitted out so as to be able to test dialectically and also to proceed as one who knows.

F45.locus: closing recapitulation of the original purpose
F45.quote: ὅπως λόγον ὑπέχοντες φυλάξομεν τὴν θέσιν ὡς δι᾿ ἐνδοξοτάτων ὁμοτρόπως
F45.claim: A further aim is how, when giving an account, to guard one's thesis through the most reputable premises in the same manner.

F46.locus: closing recapitulation of the original purpose
F46.quote: ἐπεὶ καὶ διὰ τοῦτο Σωκράτης ἠρώτα, ἀλλ᾿ οὐκ ἀπεκρίνετο· ὡμολόγει γὰρ οὐκ εἰδέναι.
F46.claim: Socrates asked questions and did not answer because he admitted he did not know.
F46.lineage: Socrates asked and did not answer

F47.quote: Τὸν αὐτὸν γὰρ λόγον δεῖ καλεῖν τὸν παρὰ ταὐτὸ γινόμενον
F47.claim: An argument arising from the same source of fallacy must be called the same argument.
F47.lineage: identity of arguments by source of fallacy

F48.quote: ὁ αὐτὸς δὲ λόγος τοῖς μὲν παρὰ τὴν λέξιν τοῖς δὲ παρὰ τὸ συμβεβηκὸς τοῖς δὲ παρ᾿ ἕτερον δόξειεν ἂν εἶναι διὰ τὸ μεταφερόμενον ἕκαστον μὴ ὁμοίως εἶναι δῆλον.
F48.claim: The same argument may seem to different people to fall under language, accident or another source, because it is not equally clear when transferred.
F48.lineage: one argument classified differently by different people

F49.quote: Δεῖ δὲ καὶ κατανοεῖν ὅτι πάντων τῶν λόγων οἱ μέν εἰσι ῥᾴους κατιδεῖν οἱ δὲ χαλεπώτεροι, παρὰ τί καὶ ἐν τίνι παραλογίζονται τὸν ἀκούοντα
F49.claim: Some arguments are easier, others harder, to see through, as to what they deceive the hearer by and in.
F49.lineage: arguments differ in difficulty of detection

F50.quote: ὥσπερ δοκεῖ τρόπος εὐηθέστατος εἶναι τῶν παραλογισμῶν
F50.claim: Fallacies from homonymy are held to be the silliest mode of fallacy.

F51.quote: καὶ γὰρ οἱ λόγοι σχεδὸν οἱ γελοῖοι πάντες εἰσὶ παρὰ τὴν λέξιν
F51.claim: Almost all jocular arguments depend on language.

F52.quote: Τὰ δὲ καὶ τοὺς ἐμπειροτάτους φαίνεται λανθάνειν· σημεῖον δὲ τούτων ὅτι μάχονται πολλάκις περὶ τῶν ὀνομάτων
F52.claim: Some homonymy-based fallacies escape even the most experienced, as shown by their frequent disputes about names.

F53.quote: οἱ δὲ τὸν Ζήνωνος λόγον καὶ Παρμενίδου λύουσι διὰ τὸ πολλαχῶς φάναι τὸ ἓν λέγεσθαι καὶ τὸ ὄν.
F53.claim: Some solve the argument of Zeno and Parmenides by saying that 'one' and 'being' are said in many ways.
F53.lineage: Zeno/Parmenides solved by multiple senses of one and being

F54.quote: καὶ λαβεῖν ἐν τίνι γένει, καὶ πότερον ἔλεγχος ἢ οὐκ ἔλεγχος, οὐ ῥᾴδιον ὁμοίως περὶ πάντων.
F54.claim: Determining the kind of fallacy and whether an argument is a refutation or not is not equally easy in all cases.

F55.quote: Ἔστι δὲ δριμὺς λόγος ὅστις ἀπορεῖν ποιεῖ μάλιστα· δάκνει γὰρ οὗτος μάλιστα.
F55.claim: A pungent argument is one that most produces perplexity; it bites most.

F56.quote: Ἀπορία δ᾿ ἐστὶ διττή, ἡ μὲν ἐν τοῖς συλλελογισμένοις, ὅ τι ἀνέλῃ τις τῶν ἐρωτημάτων, ἡ δ᾿ ἐν τοῖς ἐριστικοῖς, πῶς εἴπῃ τις τὸ προταθέν.
F56.claim: Perplexity is twofold: in valid arguments, which question to remove; in eristic ones, how to state the proposition.

F57.quote: Ἔστι δὲ συλλογιστικὸς μὲν λόγος δριμύτατος, ἂν ἐξ ὅτι μάλιστα δοκούντων ὅτι μάλιστα ἔνδοξον ἀναιρῇ.
F57.claim: The most pungent valid argument is one that overturns a maximally reputable view from maximally reputable premises.

F58.quote: Τῶν δ᾿ ἐριστικῶν δριμύτατος μὲν ὁ πρῶτον εὐθὺς ἄδηλος πότερον συλλελόγισται ἢ οὔ
F58.claim: The most pungent eristic argument is one where it is at first unclear whether it is a valid deduction and whether the solution lies in falsity or division.

F59.claim: An argument that is not a valid deduction is sometimes not to be despised.

F60.quote: ἀλλ᾿ ὁ μὲν λόγος ἐπιεικής, ὁ δ᾿ ἐρωτῶν ἠρώτηκεν οὐ καλῶς.
F60.claim: Where the missing element is external, the argument is decent but the questioner has questioned badly.

F61.quote: ὥσπερ λύειν ὁτὲ μὲν πρὸς τὸν λόγον ὁτὲ δὲ πρὸς τὸν ἐρωτῶντα καὶ τὴν ἐρώτησιν ὁτὲ δὲ πρὸς οὐδέτερον τούτων
F61.claim: A solution may be directed at the argument, at the questioner and question, or at neither; likewise questioning may be directed at the thesis, the answerer or the time.
F61.lineage: solutions directed at argument, questioner or neither

F62.quote: Ἐκ πόσων μὲν οὖν καὶ ποίων γίνονται τοῖς διαλεγομένοις οἱ παραλογισμοί, καὶ πῶς δείξομέν τε ψευδόμενον
F62.claim: The author summarises what has been covered: sources of fallacies, refuting and leading to paradox, premises, ordering of questions, uses, answering, and solving arguments.

F63.quote: Ὅτι μὲν οὖν ἔχει τέλος ἱκανῶς ἃ προειλόμεθα, φανερόν
F63.claim: It is clear that what was undertaken has been adequately completed.

F64.quote: Ταύτης δὲ τῆς πραγματείας οὐ τὸ μὲν ἦν τὸ δ᾿ οὐκ ἦν προεξειργασμένον, ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν.
F64.claim: For this inquiry nothing at all had been worked out previously.
F64.lineage: no predecessors for the theory of syllogism and refutation

F65.quote: περὶ δὲ τοῦ συλλογίζεσθαι παντελῶς οὐδὲν εἴχομεν πρότερον ἄλλο λέγειν, ἀλλ᾿ ἢ τριβῇ ζητοῦντες πολὺν χρόνον ἐπονοῦμεν.
F65.claim: On reasoning there was nothing previously to cite; the author laboured long by trial and inquiry.
F65.lineage: no predecessors for the theory of syllogism and refutation

F66.quote: Μέγιστον γὰρ ἴσως ἀρχὴ παντός, ὥσπερ λέγεται· διὸ καὶ χαλεπώτατον
F66.claim: A beginning is perhaps the greatest part of everything, and hence the hardest; discoveries made from scratch grow little at first but are far more useful than later growth.

F67.quote: Τισίας μὲν μετὰ τοὺς πρώτους, Θρασύμαχος δὲ μετὰ Τισίαν, Θεόδωρος δὲ μετὰ τοῦτον
F67.claim: Rhetoric grew by succession: Tisias after the first, Thrasymachus after Tisias, Theodorus after him.

F68.locus: closing, on paid teachers of eristic
F68.quote: Καὶ γὰρ τῶν περὶ τοὺς ἐριστικοὺς λόγους μισθαρνούντων ὁμοία τις ἦν ἡ παίδευσις τῇ Γοργίου πραγματείᾳ.
F68.claim: The paid teachers of eristic arguments used an education similar to Gorgias' practice, handing over arguments to memorise.
F68.lineage: paid teachers taught by memorised arguments

F69.locus: closing, on paid teachers of eristic
F69.quote: οὐ γὰρ τέχνην ἀλλὰ τὰ ἀπὸ τῆς τέχνης διδόντες παιδεύειν ὑπελάμβανον
F69.claim: Their teaching was quick but artless: they gave the products of an art, not the art, and thought they were educating.
F69.lineage: teaching products of the art rather than the art

F70.quote: ὥσπερ ἂν εἴ τις ἐπιστήμην φάσκων παραδώσειν ἐπὶ τὸ μηδὲν πονεῖν τοὺς πόδας, εἶτα σκυτοτομικὴν μὲν μὴ διδάσκοι
F70.claim: Like someone promising to spare the feet pain who gives many kinds of shoes but does not teach shoemaking: he met the need but passed on no art.

F71.quote: δεῖ δ᾿ ἡμᾶς μὴ λεληθέναι τὸ συμβεβηκὸς περὶ ταύτην τὴν πραγματείαν.
F71.claim: We must keep in mind the condition attending this inquiry, namely that it began from nothing.
F71.lineage: limit: pioneering status of the work

F72.quote: λοιπὸν ἂν εἴη πάντων ὑμῶν ἢ τῶν ἠκροαμένων ἔργον τοῖς μὲν παραλελειμμένοις τῆς μεθόδου συγγνώμην τοῖς δ᾿ εὑρημένοις πολλὴν ἔχειν χάριν.
F72.claim: If the method seems adequate given its starting point, it remains for the audience to forgive its omissions and be warmly grateful for what has been discovered.
F72.lineage: limit: pioneering status of the work

L_B.text: Sophistical Refutations is Aristotle's treatise on apparent refutation: per Pickard-Cambridge, it states its subject as "sophistic refutations, i.e. what appear to be refutations but are really fallacies instead". The treatise defines reasoning and refutation, and extends the sophistical sense to reasoning that is valid but only appears appropriate to the thing in question. It treats the sophist's art as "the semblance of wisdom without the reality". It divides fallacies into six dependent on language and seven independent of it, and says names are the chief source because names are finite and things infinite. The art of examining is a branch of dialectic, and a field source reads the work as an appendix to the Topics and places it in the Organon grouping of the ancient commentators. The work closes with a recapitulation of its aim, a syllogistic capacity from endoxa, with Socrates asking and not answering. Its last chapter states that of this inquiry "οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν", contrasts rhetoric's succession with paid teachers who gave products and not the art, and ends on its own pioneering limit.

L_BA.text: Sophistical Refutations is Aristotle's treatise on apparent refutation: per the translation of Pickard-Cambridge, it states its subject as "sophistic refutations, i.e. what appear to be refutations but are really fallacies instead". The treatise defines reasoning as resting on "certain statements such that they involve necessarily the assertion of something other than what has been stated, through what has been stated", and refutation as "reasoning involving the contradictory of the given conclusion". It extends the definition: a sophistical refutation and syllogism is one that "appears to be valid but is not" and also one which, "though it is valid, only appears to be appropriate to the thing in question". The art of the sophist is defined there as "the semblance of wisdom without the reality", and contentious arguments as those that reason or appear to reason from premisses that appear to be generally accepted but are not. The treatise itself places demonstrative arguments in the Analytics and dialectic and examination arguments elsewhere, and a field source reads the work as "a final section, or an appendix, to the Topics", a reading it holds as interpretation. The grouping of the work in an Organon is attributed by the same field source to "the ancient commentators", and that source adds that "Aristotle himself never uses this term". The treatise states a two-fold division: "two styles of refutation: for some depend on the language used, while some are independent of language". Six depend on language, listed as "ambiguity, amphiboly, combination, division of words, accent, form of expression", and seven are independent of it. Language is given its weight by a statement of the work: "the most prolific and usual domain is the argument that turns upon names only", because "names are finite and so is the sum-total of formulae, while things are infinite in number", so that a single name has a number of meanings. Its examples include the ambiguity of "learn" in "Those learn who know" and the accident fallacy of Coriscus, who if different from "man" would be "different from himself: for he is a man". Archive deposit 1697 reads the article's later Fallacies section as a conversion: its labels contradict its list, and a stated criterion becomes membership in a later taxonomy. That reading is paired in the deposit with the finding that the narrowing is unsound against the article's own sources, and the edit history records the section's labels as one editor's own reading of the text. The treatise distinguishes examination from sophistry: the art of examining is a branch of dialectic, while sophistic refutations, even when they prove the contradictory of a thesis, do not make clear whether the answerer is ignorant. A dialectician is one who "regards the common principles with their application to the particular matter in hand", and one who only appears to do so is a sophist. The treatise says it is possible "to hold an examination on everything" by an art that "is not of the same kind as those which demonstrate". It lists five aims of contentious disputants, ending with reducing the opponent to babbling. Krabbe, cited in deposit 1697, calls it "a useful treatise for sophists" who "should study fallacies not to avoid them, but rather to commit them when it suits their purposes"; the deposit finds the article's opposition between dialectic and sophistry in tension with that reading. The same deposit reads the article's lead as substituting a truth-normative pattern for the endoxic capacity and as dropping the premisses, which are the programme's scope. Deposit 1585 reads the work stylometrically as a registry of what people do in argument, a candidate reading it states as a hypothesis, and deposits 1585 and 1586 place it at the world pole of the first axis, while a file erratum in 1586 puts the real text on the apparatus side. The work ends in chapter 34 with a recapitulation of the aim, in the Greek: "Προειλόμεθα μὲν οὖν εὑρεῖν δύναμίν τινα συλλογιστικὴν περὶ τοῦ προβληθέντος ἐκ τῶν ὑπαρχόντων ὡς ἐνδοξοτάτων". The work of that capacity is given as dialectic's and the peirastic's: "τοῦτο γὰρ ἔργον ἐστὶ τῆς διαλεκτικῆς καθ᾿ αὑτὴν καὶ τῆς πειραστικῆς", and the text adds that sophistic's proximity shapes the discipline. Deposit 1697 reads the epilogue as an accounting of a capacity (δύναμις) for dialectic and peirastic. The chapter holds that Socrates "asked and did not answer": "Σωκράτης ἠρώτα, ἀλλ᾿ οὐκ ἀπεκρίνετο· ὡμολόγει γὰρ οὐκ εἰδέναι". Deposit 1603 reads this as either the artless examining everyone shares, from which nothing is received, or something the epilogue files under the inquiry's own purposes, and on neither reading as an antecedent source. The chapter then states, in the Greek of 183b34-36: "Ταύτης δὲ τῆς πραγματείας οὐ τὸ μὲν ἦν τὸ δ᾿ οὐκ ἦν προεξειργασμένον, ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν." It adds, of syllogizing: "περὶ δὲ τοῦ συλλογίζεσθαι παντελῶς οὐδὲν εἴχομεν πρότερον ἄλλο λέγειν, ἀλλ᾿ ἢ τριβῇ ζητοῦντες πολὺν χρόνον ἐπονοῦμεν". Deposit 1603 reads the sentence literally, as denying that anything of the inquiry existed beforehand, and holds that the closing chapter is built joint by joint so that the sentence can be kept. The deposit finds the transmission vocabulary, παρ᾽ ἑτέρων, ἐκ διαδοχῆς, ἐκ παραδόσεως, freshly used with three lines of names attached, and held in no instance of Socrates, and it reads the origination vocabulary ἐξ ὑπαρχῆς, ἐξ ἀρχῆς likewise. Deposit 1603 reads the ending as performing the peirastic operation on its reader: a reader who qualifies the sentence supplies what the text was written without, and does not perceive the supplying. The deposit disclaims any design: it does not claim the chapter was built as a trap, since structures do not need intentions to function. Deposit 1603 leaves Socrates' possession of the art where the chapter leaves it. The chapter divides discoveries by provenance: rhetoric advanced by succession, "Τισίας μὲν μετὰ τοὺς πρώτους, Θρασύμαχος δὲ μετὰ Τισίαν, Θεόδωρος δὲ μετὰ τοῦτον". The paid teachers of eristic are likened to the instruction of Gorgias, and the text says they gave "οὐ γὰρ τέχνην ἀλλὰ τὰ ἀπὸ τῆς τέχνης", the products of the art and not the art. The text illustrates this with a shoemaker analogy: one who promised knowledge to spare the feet pain, and taught no shoemaking. The work closes by naming its own pioneering condition: "δεῖ δ᾿ ἡμᾶς μὴ λεληθέναι τὸ συμβεβηκὸς περὶ ταύτην τὴν πραγματείαν", and by asking its hearers for indulgence toward omissions and thanks for what has been found. Translators of the closing sentence render it whole, according to deposit 1603: the narrowing, to "no systematic treatment" or "no completed art", enters in the gloss. Poste's note, as quoted in a blog catalogue record, finds it "difficult to reconcile Aristotle's assertion with what we know had been done by Plato and Socrates and the Eleatics and Megarians"; the record reads the premise as what we know and the sentence as what must be reconciled with it. The archive's tension with Prior Analytics I.31, where Aristotle calls division, practised throughout the Platonic dialogues, part of the inquiry, is stated in deposit 1576 and is read there as a tension and not as a refutation. A blog record reports that across twenty rounds of simulated review, each round inserted a qualifier into the sentence, and that the terminal round endorsed a sentence that is Aristotle's with the particle οὐ removed. The record reads this as the reception deleting the negation at composition, unperceived, as Sophistical Refutations 16 predicts, and as restoring provenance from others. The article's lead states the work's priority as an attribute; deposit 1696 reads the sentence "about syllogizing we had absolutely nothing else earlier to say" as becoming "the first work to treat the subject of deductive reasoning", a total negation over a stated domain turned into a property, primacy. Deposit 1697 reads this conversion as the clearest of the article's changes, and records its edit history as the composition of two edits that ran opposite ways. On the same article, deposit 1697 finds the claim of exhaustiveness hedged by a footnote folded into the text, "Sometimes listed as twelve.", added in a 2025 edit. The same deposit records that other sentences of the article stay faithful to their source, finding no attributization in them. Deposit 1697 notes that no discussion of the lead, the gloss, the qualifier or the labels has ever taken place on the talk page. Deposit 1576 states that the priority claim sits in tension with Prior Analytics I.31; deposit 1579 traces the edition of a received Socrates in the Second Letter into Aristotle's epilogue at SE 34 and leaves open whether such an edition implies anything about how many hands made the texts. Deposit 1587 holds that the two names Aristotle and Theophrastus fail as two authors and leaves the maker-count open.
